### 1. Start by listening, not adjusting

Then discuss concrete scenarios: How will she handle communication in meetings? What accommodations will she request, and how? What networks or mentors who are Deaf/HoH can she connect to?

Instead of saying “You probably won’t be able to do X,” share a balanced view:

> *“I’ve seen Deaf colleagues thrive in roles like Y and Z. Some fields, like A, currently have more barriers, but people are breaking those down. Let’s look at your strengths and what environments would set you up to do your best work.”*

### 4. Encourage her to research Deaf professionals in her dream field
Representation matters. If she can see herself in someone else’s success story, that’s powerful. Suggest she reach out to them directly through professional Deaf networks.

### 5. Be transparent about your own learning edge
If you’re hearing and haven’t worked extensively with Deaf professionals, it’s okay to say:

> *“I’m still learning about the best ways to support your career path. I never want to lowball what you can achieve. Will you help me understand what support looks like from your perspective?”*
